docs.title: Lizard
docs.text:
Lizard is a domain-specific language to define hardware behavior. It is intended to run on embedded systems which are connected to motor controllers, sensors etc. Most of the time it is used in combination with a higher level engine like ROS or RoSys. You can think of the microcontroller as the machine's lizard brain which ensures basic safety and performs all time-critical actions.

The idea is to not compile and deploy specific C++ code for every new hardware requirement. Instead you simply write your commands in a text-based language which can be changed on the fly.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Shell-like input and output over serial communication to ease the development
  • Quick and resource-efficient execution on embedded hardware
  • Built-in checksums to detect transmission errors
  • Safety conditions that are checked continuously
  • Ability to work across multiple microcontrollers
  • Human-readable and easy-to-type (like Python)
  • Persistent "startup" commands to apply configuration after boot

docs.title: Concept
docs.text:
Lizard consists of individual hardware modules that are either defined in a persistent startup script or interactively via console input. Each module has a name, a number of required or optional constructor arguments and possibly a step function as well as a number of properties.

Furthermore, Lizard allows to define rules, possibly asynchronous routines and variables. A routine is simply a collection of Lizard statements. If a rule's condition evaluates to true, the corresponding routine is started. Conditions can involve variables, module properties and constant expressions.

One core module is automatically defined first. It provides interaction with the microcontroller itself, e.g. reading the system's time or causing a restart.

During a main loop Lizard repeatedly performs the following tasks:

  1. Read and evaluate input from the serial interface.
  2. Run the step functions of each module in the order of their creation, the core module last.
  3. Check all rules and execute associated routines.
  4. Advance routines that are already running and waiting for certain conditions.
  5. Send the telemetry frames that are due.

docs.title: Turn on an LED
docs.text:
Create a new LED "green" at pin 14 and turn it on:

green = Output(14)
green.on()

docs.title: Read a button
docs.text:
Create a button "b1" at pin 25 with internal pull-up resistor and read its value:

b1 = Input(25)
b1.pullup()
b1.level

docs.title: Write a persistent startup script
docs.text:
Clear the persistent storage, configure a button and an LED, write the new startup script to the persistent storage, restart the microcontroller with these two new modules and print the stored configuration:

!-
!+green = Output(14)
!+b1 = Input(25)
!.
core.restart()
!?

docs.title: Define a rule
docs.text:
Create an LED "red", a button "b1" with pull-up resistor as well as a condition "c1" that turns off the LED as soon as the button is pressed:

red = Output(14)
red.on()
b1 = Input(25)
b1.pullup()
when b1.level == 0 then red.off(); end

docs.title: Create a shadow module
docs.text:
Create a "green" LED that shadows a "red" LED, i.e. will receive a copy of each command:

green = Output(13)
red = Output(14)
red.shadow(green)

docs.title: Use a port expander
docs.text:
Create a serial connection as well as a port expander with an LED at pin 15 and turn it on:

serial = Serial(26, 27, 11500, 1)
expander = Expander(serial, 32, 33)
led = expander.Output(15)
led.on()

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
1. Download and unpack the zip file of the latest release.
  2. Attach an Espressif ESP32 microcontroller via serial to your computer.
  3. Run sudo ./espresso.py flash to install Lizard on the ESP32. Add --device /dev/<serial device name> to pick the adapter yourself, for example when several are attached.

docs.title: Try Out
docs.text:
You can launch an interactive shell with ./monitor.py to try out configurations and watch Lizard outputs (see tools for more details). To verify that the communication is working, use one of the following commands to generate some output:

core.info()
core.millis
core.print("Hello, Lizard!")

See the module reference for other commands.

To try out individual modules, you can get their current properties or unmute them for continuous output, e.g.:

estop = Input(34)
estop.level
estop.unmute()

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text: Of course you should connect the ESP32 to some hardware you want to control. From basic pins like LEDs (see Output) and buttons (see Input) to communication via CAN and control of stepper motors.

docs.title: Startup Script
docs.text:
You can create a startup script for rules which should be directly applied after boot of the microcontroller. Simply write the commands into a file like on_startup.lizard and set them with

./configure.py on_startup.lizard

Add the device path (e.g. ./configure.py on_startup.lizard /dev/<serial device name>) to pick the adapter yourself, for example when several are attached.

See Tools for more details.

If loading the startup script fails, for example because a module cannot be created, the microcontroller prints the error and restarts to try again. After two failed attempts it boots without the startup script, prints error: startup skipped after 2 failed boots (...) with the last reason and stays reachable over the command-line interface, so the script can be fixed with !-, !+ and !.. A node whose console is the link of a serial bus stays reachable over the bus instead, through its coordinator, once a startup script with that bus has run through and left its bus backup. A crash or watchdog reset during the first seconds after boot counts as a failed attempt as well. A power cycle or a reset over the EN pin clears the counter.

docs.title: Statements
docs.text:
Statements are input via the command-line interface or stored in the startup script on the microcontroller. The following statement types are currently supported.

Expressions

An expression can be a constant value, a variable, a module property, an arithmetic or logical expression as well as various combinations:

true
42
3.14
"Hello world"
led
button.level
1 + (2 - 3 * 4)**5
1 == 2 or (x == 4 and button.level == 0)

Expressions can be assigned to variables, used in conditions and passed to constructors, method calls or routine calls. Plain expression statements print their result to the command line. Expressions can be nested up to 39 levels deep, where every operator and every pair of parentheses adds a level. A chain like a + b + c + ... can therefore have up to 40 terms. Deeper expressions are rejected with "expression is nested too deeply".

Variables: declaration and assignment

New variables need to be explicitly declared with a data type:

int i

They can be immediately initialized:

int i = 1

Otherwise they have an initial value of false, 0, 0.0 or "", respectively.

Variables can be assigned a new value of compatible data type:

i = 2

Modules: constructors, method calls and property assignments

Constructors are used to create module instances:

led = Output(15)

See the module reference for more details about individual modules and their argument lists.

Constructors can also be used with expander modules to instantiate a remote module that can be controlled from the main microcontroller:

led = expander.Output(15)

You can call module methods as follows:

led.on()

Some module properties are meant to be written to:

motor.reversed = true

Properties: declaration

Some modules accept property declarations, which work like variable declarations:

float x.level = 0.5

Modules that do not accept declarations report an error. Proxies and BusTelemetry modules accept declarations.

Routines: definition and call

Routines have a name and contain a list of actions:

let all_on do
    green.on()
    red.on()
end

They can be called similar to module methods:

all_on()

Rules: definition

Rules execute a list of actions when a condition is met:

when button.level == 0 then
    core.print("Off!")
    led.off()
end

In contrast to an if-statement known from other languages a when-condition is checked in every cycle of Lizard's main loop. Whenever the condition is true, the actions are executed.

Note that actions can be asynchronous. If there are still actions running asynchronously, a truthy condition is ignored.

Scheduled blocks

Scheduled blocks execute a list of actions once at a given time, specified in milliseconds since boot (matching core.millis):

at 125015 do
    en3.on()
end

The time expression is evaluated once when the statement is interpreted, so relative times can be expressed with core.millis:

at core.millis + 500 do en3.off() end

In contrast to rules and routines, scheduled blocks fire with millisecond precision, decoupled from the main loop. This allows streaming time-critical sequences like trajectory setpoints from a host system.

Each scheduled block is executed exactly once and discarded afterwards. If the time is already in the past, the actions are executed immediately. Blocks with equal times fire in the order of their definition.

await is not allowed inside scheduled blocks. A scheduled block can, however, call a routine that itself awaits conditions or routines: the routine starts at the scheduled time and continues with Lizard's regular main loop cycle.

At most 100 scheduled blocks can be pending at the same time; further at statements fail with the error message "schedule is full". All pending blocks can be discarded with core.clear_schedule(), for example when the connection to the host system is lost (see machine safety).

When core.debug is true, each firing reports its lateness, e.g. at 125015: fired 0.3 ms late.

docs.title: Actions
docs.text:
Routines and rules contain a list of actions.

Method and routine calls

Like with a method call statement, you can call methods and routines with an action:

when clicked then
    core.print("On!")
    all_on()
end

Property and variable assignments

Like with the corresponding assignment statements, you can assign properties and variables with an action as well:

when i > 0 then
    i = 0
    core.debug = true
end

Await conditions and routines

In contrast to statements, actions can await conditions, causing the execution of subsequent actions to wait until the condition is met.

int t
let blink do
    t = core.millis
    led.on()
    await core.millis > t + 1000
    led.off()
end

Similarly, actions can await asynchronous routines, causing subsequent actions to wait until a routine is completed.

when button.level == 0 then
    core.print("Blink...")
    await blink()
    core.print("Done.")
end

Failing actions

If an action fails, for example because a module reports an error, the error is printed and the remaining actions are skipped. The rule or routine has then finished: a rule fires again the next time its condition is true and starts again from its first action, and a routine can be called again. A rule that uses a flag to fire only once should therefore set the flag after its actions; otherwise a failed action is never attempted again. If an awaited routine fails, the await fails as well and the actions after it are skipped. A routine started without await runs on its own, so its failure does not affect the rule or routine that started it.

docs.title: Data types
docs.text:
Lizard currently supports five data types:

Data type Example Range boolean bool b = true false, true integer number int i = 0 64-bit unsigned integer floating point number float f = 0.0 64-bit float string str s = "foo" identifier led = Output(15)

Note that identifiers cannot be created via variable declarations, but only via constructors.

Floating point numbers can also be nan (not a number) and inf (infinity), both as literals and in outputs; every comparison with nan is false except !=, which is always true, so x != x tests for nan. Like true and false, nan and inf are reserved words and cannot be used as variable or module names.

Implicit conversion only happens from integers to floating point numbers:

int i = 42
float f = i + 3.14

docs.title: Whitespace, comments and line breaks
docs.text:
Tabs and spaces are treated as whitespace.

Blank lines are interpreted as no-op and do nothing.

Line comments start with #.

Multiple statements or actions are separated with ; or a newline.

docs.title: Control commands
docs.text:
Lines with a leading ! can indicate one of the following control commands.

Command Meaning !+abc Add abc to the startup script !-abc Remove lines starting with abc from the startup script !? Print the startup script !. Write the startup script to non-volatile storage !!abc Interpret abc as Lizard code !"abc Print abc to the command-line

Note that !+ and !- edit a copy of the startup script in RAM, which is only written to non-volatile storage with the !. command; until then !? prints this copy. Otherwise the startup script is not held in RAM: !? reads it from non-volatile storage, and the boot runs it from there statement by statement. The !. command does not reply when it succeeds and prints an error when it cannot write to non-volatile storage. The core.startup_checksum() command sums the bytes of the copy while there is one, so before !. it checks the result of the !+ and !- commands. After a successful !. there is no copy, and the same command sums what !. has stored, also before a restart. If !. fails, the copy stays in RAM for another !., and core.startup_checksum() reports the error instead of a checksum until the copy changes or a !. succeeds. If the stored script cannot be read, !+ and !-abc report the error and change nothing; !- starts a new script without reading the old one.

Input from the default command-line interface UART0 is usually interpreted as Lizard code; input from a port expander is usually printed to the command-line on UART0. This behavior can be changed using !! and !".

docs.title: Machine Safety
docs.text: Lizard implements the following features to increase machine safety.

docs.title: Checksums
docs.text:
Each line sent via the command-line interface can and should be followed by a checksum. Lizard will omit any lines with incorrect checksums. Any output is as well sent with a checksum. Lines are limited to 2048 bytes in either direction, including the checksum and the line ending. Lizard discards a longer input line and replaces a longer output line, each with a warning.

The 8-bit checksum is computed as the bitwise XOR of all bytes of the UTF-8 encoded line excluding the newline character and written as a two-digit hex number (with leading zeros) separated with an @ character, for example:

Line Bitwise XOR Result 1 + 2 0x31 ^ 0x20 ^ 0x2b ^ 0x20 ^ 0x32 = 0x28 1 + 2@28

docs.title: Keep-alive signal
docs.text:
The core module provides a property last_message_age, which holds the time in milliseconds since the last input message was received from the host via UART0 or Bluetooth. It allows formulating rules that stop critical hardware modules when the connection to the host system is lost.

The following example stops a motor when there is no serial communication for 500 ms:

when core.last_message_age > 500 then motor.stop(); end

Any message from UART0 or Bluetooth that is not discarded due to an invalid checksum resets last_message_age, even if it cannot be parsed. Messages received over the serial bus do not reset it, so a peer pushing its state to the core cannot implicitly mask a lost host connection. If the host controller has no command to send but wants to signal that it is still alive, it can call core.keep_alive(), which resets the timer silently without producing any output. This also works over the serial bus: a coordinator can keep a peer's timer alive by explicitly sending it core.keep_alive().

If the host streams scheduled blocks, they should be discarded as well when the connection is lost, so that no stale commands fire after the host stopped:

when core.last_message_age > 500 then motor.stop(); core.clear_schedule() end

If an action fails, the remaining actions of the rule are skipped (see failing actions). In the example above, a failing motor.stop() would keep the schedule from being cleared. Safety actions that do not depend on each other therefore belong in separate rules:

when core.last_message_age > 500 then motor.stop(); end
when core.last_message_age > 500 then core.clear_schedule(); end

docs.title: Dead man's switch for wheels
docs.text:
The keep-alive rule above has a blind spot: core.last_message_age is reset by any input line, on any channel. A robot that is driven by a remote control over Bluetooth while a host keeps sending heartbeats over UART0 therefore never trips such a rule when the Bluetooth connection drops, and keeps driving with the last speed it received.

The wheels modules (ODrive Wheels, RoboClaw Wheels and DunkerWheels) therefore carry their own dead man's switch that measures what actually matters: the time since the last drive command to that module, whichever channel it came from.

wheels.drive_command_timeout = 0.3

After a non-zero speed() or power() command, the wheels stop on their own once no further drive command arrived for drive_command_timeout seconds. Only drive commands count; enable(), off() or property writes cannot keep a stale motion alive. The stop is logged as a warning and held like the locked interlock holds, with the zero-speed setpoint refreshed about once per second, so a stop that did not reach the motors — a failing motor send, a dropped CAN frame, a restarting motor controller — is re-asserted. The next drive command releases the hold and re-arms the switch, so a reconnecting sender has to issue a fresh command before the robot moves again. The default timeout is 1 s as a defensive baseline; 0 disables the switch, e.g. on a test bench.

Consequently, a host that wants to keep driving has to repeat its drive command at least once per timeout. A single delayed command can move the robot for at most one timeout. Choose the timeout as a trade-off between the stopping distance at full speed and false stops on short radio dropouts: a sender that nominally transmits every 100 ms but skips cycles while a write is pending needs a timeout of a few hundred milliseconds.

A stop that the wheels did send counts as a stop for the switch, so a zero that got lost on the bus or was refused by a drive would otherwise never be caught: the wheels would creep at their last setpoint until the next command. Therefore a speed(0, 0) after motion, including the one that releases a tripped switch, is repeated about every 100 ms for one second. Any other speed(), power() or off() that goes through ends the repeat early, and so do locked, a tripped switch and disabling the wheels, which hold or stop the wheels on their own. The ODrive Wheels section of the module reference describes the details.

The drive_command_age property (ms) and the Bluetooth module's connected and last_message_age properties expose the underlying measurements for rules and logging.

docs.title: Expander watchdog
docs.text:
The expander module provides a watchdog feature that detects when the port expander gets stuck and does not send messages anymore. After ping_interval seconds of no messages from the port expander, the expander module will instruct the expander to send a "__PONG__" message. If the expander does not answer within ping_timeout seconds, the expander and its proxies are marked as not ready (is_ready turns false).

The reception of the "__PONG__" message is handled internally by the expander module and is not printed to the serial output. A similar technique can be used by the main computing unit to check if the core microcontroller is still responsive and restart it otherwise.

If a proxy module is active, the ping_interval will never elapse, because the expander module receives messages via the proxy message handling. Thus it will not need to ping the expander explicitly.

docs.title: Module Reference
docs.text:
All Lizard modules have the following methods in common.

Methods Description module.mute() Turn output off module.unmute() Turn output on module.shadow() Send all method calls also to another module module.broadcast() Regularly send properties to another microcontroller (for internal use)

Shadows are useful if multiple modules should behave exactly the same, e.g. two actuators that should always move synchronously.

The broadcast method is used internally with port expanders.

A module reserves the pins and peripherals it uses on its microcontroller, i.e. GPIO pins, UART ports, the CAN controller and ADC units, until the core restarts. I2C modules on the same port share its SDA and SCL pins, which stay reserved for that port. Creating a module on a reserved pin or peripheral fails with an error that names the owner, e.g. pin 15 is already used by module "led". In the startup script, such an error stops the script like any other error (see Startup Script). The console UART with its pins and the pins of the SPI flash are reserved from the start. Only a serial bus can take over the console UART (see Console as Link).

docs.title: Core
docs.text:
The core module encapsulates various properties and methods that are related to the microcontroller itself. It is automatically created right after the boot sequence.

Properties Description Data type core.debug Whether to output debug information to the command line bool core.millis Time since booting the microcontroller (ms) int core.heap Free heap memory (bytes) int core.last_message_age Time since last input message was received and interpreted (ms) int Methods Description Arguments core.restart() Restart the microcontroller core.version() Show project name and version core.info() Show project name, project version (and Lizard version if different), compile time and IDF version core.print(...) Print arbitrary arguments to the command line arbitrary core.output(format) Define the output format str core.startup_checksum() Show 16-bit checksum of the startup script (sum of its UTF-8 bytes), or the error of a failed !. core.get_pin_status(pin) Print the status of the chosen pin int core.set_pin_level(pin, value) Turns the pin into an output and sets its level int, int core.get_pin_strapping(pin) Print value of the pin from the strapping register int core.forget_serial_bus() Remove the saved SerialBus configuration from NVS core.set_baudrate(baud) Persist UART0 baud rate (applied after restart) int core.pause_broadcasts() Pause property broadcasts (all modules) core.resume_broadcasts() Resume property broadcasts core.clear_schedule() Discard all pending scheduled blocks core.keep_alive() Reset last_message_age without producing output core.telemetry(...) Define a telemetry frame of properties and variables see below core.telemetry_info() Send the layout lines of all telemetry frames again and ask passed-on bus peers for theirs core.clear_telemetry() Clear all telemetry frames

The output format is a string with multiple space-separated elements of the pattern <module>.<property>[:<precision>] or <variable>[:<precision>]. The precision is an optional integer specifying the number of decimal places for a floating point number. For example, the format "core.millis input.level motor.position:3" might yield an output like "92456 1 12.789". An empty format "" stops the core line until a new format is set.

core.get_pin_status(pin) reads the pin's voltage, not the output state directly.

UART baud rate: The console (UART0) defaults to 115200 baud. core.set_baudrate(baud) persists a new rate to non-volatile storage; it takes effect on the next restart, so the change is not a breaking one for hosts that are not updated yet. After core.set_baudrate(921600) followed by core.restart(), reconnect with the host tools at the new rate, e.g. ./monitor.py /dev/ttyUSB0 --baud 921600 (monitor.py, configure.py and otb_update.py all accept --baud, defaulting to 115200). Supported rates are 115200, 230400, 460800, 921600, 1000000, 1500000, 2000000 and 3000000. Above 921600, check which rates the host's UART actually produces: a Jetson Orin, for example, produces 1000000, 1500000 and 3000000 exactly, but 2000000 about 2 % too slow. Some USB-UART bridges stop below 3000000. The host's UART also has to keep up with the rate: a Jetson whose UART received without DMA lost 5 to 20 % of the core's lines at 1500000 to 3000000 (see discussion #260), while with RX DMA enabled in its device tree it ran clean up to 3000000. If the host cannot talk to the core at the new rate, erase the chip with ./espresso.py erase and flash it again. Erasing also clears the startup script and the other settings stored in non-volatile storage, so configure the core again afterwards. Note that the ROM bootloader and the early boot log always use 115200 regardless of this setting, so pre-application boot output will look garbled at higher rates.

Console load: Sending a line blocks the main loop until its bytes are on the wire, so at 115200 baud only about 115 bytes fit into one 10 ms cycle. When printing is what stretches at least half of the cycles well past their 10 ms for three seconds in a row, Lizard warns, e.g. warning: printing stretched the loop to 83 ms, the console baud rate is too low for its output, at most once a minute. Print less, for example by broadcasting fewer proxies, or raise the baud rate. On an expander the console is its serial link to the core: the warning arrives there with the expander's name in front, e.g. p: warning: …, and the rate in question is that of the link, not the core's UART0.

Telemetry frames: core.telemetry(...) sends properties and variables in binary form, as one line per frame next to the text lines on the console. Layout lines name and type the fields, so a reader needs no configuration.

core.telemetry(imu.yaw, imu.pitch, imu.temp)                   # frame 1, every step
core.telemetry(wheels.linear_speed, wheels.angular_speed, 20)  # frame 2, every 20 ms

Each call defines one frame, or several if its values take more than 180 bytes (see below); frame IDs count up from 1 in the order of definition. The arguments are properties or variables of type bool, int or float, and a field may appear in several calls, but only once per call. A field's name, <module>.<property> or the variable's name, has at most 200 characters. An integer literal as last argument is the interval in milliseconds (0 to 3600000); an int variable or property in that place is a field. Without an interval or with 0, the frame is sent every step. Frames go out with the 10 ms steps, so the gaps between them vary, e.g. 10 and 20 ms for an interval of 15 ms, but match the interval on average. Frames are built at the end of the step, after modules, rules and routines, so all fields of a frame come from the same step. The values of one frame take at most 180 bytes, e.g. 45 floats. A call whose values take more is split into several frames, each filled up in the order of the arguments, with its own frame ID and layout. These frames share their timer and are sent in the same step, only once all of them are announced, so they carry the same millis and a reader can merge them into one step by that time. Every one of them counts against the limit of 255 frames. core.clear_telemetry() removes all frames and frees their IDs.

A frame line is ~<base64>@xx: a tilde, the Base64 encoding of the frame body (standard alphabet with = padding) and the usual checksum.

Bytes Content 1 frame ID 1 layout ID, see below 1 sequence number per frame ID, modulo 256; a gap means lost frames 4 time since booting (ms) when the frame was built n values of the fields 2 CRC-16/CCITT-FALSE over all preceding bytes

The sequence number starts at 0 when a frame is defined, also when its ID is reused after core.clear_telemetry(). The float and int fields come first, in the order of the arguments: a float as float32, an int as its low 32 bits, so a value beyond the int32 range wraps around instead of sticking at the limit. Every reader, the host decoder included, reads them as int32. Send an age rather than a timestamp: a timestamp in µs like last_heartbeat of a CANopen motor turns negative after 36 minutes, and a host reads the time of the sender from the header anyway. The bool fields follow as bits in their order, least significant bit first, padded to a full byte. All multi-byte numbers, including the time and the CRC, are little-endian.

A layout line __LAYOUT__v1 <frame>.<index>/<count> <layout ID> <name>:<type> describes one field: its frame ID, its position from 0, the number of fields in the frame, the layout ID in two hex digits, its name and its type: f for float, i for int or ? for bool. For example, core.telemetry(motor.position, motor.axis_state, motor.enabled) yields:

__LAYOUT__v1 1.0/3 bf motor.position:f@4a
__LAYOUT__v1 1.1/3 bf motor.axis_state:i@76
__LAYOUT__v1 1.2/3 bf motor.enabled:?@6d
~Ab8HQOIBALbznT8IAAAAAY/t@25

The frame body 01 bf 07 40e20100 b6f39d3f 08000000 01 8fed holds frame ID 1, layout ID bf, sequence number 7, millis 123456, the values 1.234, 8 and true, and the CRC.

The layout ID is the low byte of the CRC-16/CCITT-FALSE over the fields as <name>:<type>, separated by spaces, here motor.position:f motor.axis_state:i motor.enabled:?. A reader decodes a frame only with layout lines of the same frame ID and layout ID, so a frame ID that core.clear_telemetry() frees and a new frame reuses is not decoded with the old fields. Different fields get the same layout ID with a chance of 1 in 256.

Layout lines go out when a frame is defined and on core.telemetry_info(), four per step in the order of the frames. A new frame is sent for the first time once all of its layout lines are out. Frames that are already running keep coming while core.telemetry_info() repeats their layout lines, except on a serial bus peer, see Serial Bus. There is no timer for them: a host that connects later or logs for hours calls core.telemetry_info() itself. On a serial bus peer, frames and layout lines go to the coordinator once it polls the peer, see Serial Bus. Only the prefix ~ and the word __LAYOUT__ stay the same in future versions of the format; the version is part of each layout line. On the host, the lizard_host package decodes these lines.

docs.title: Bluetooth
docs.text:
Lizard can receive messages via Bluetooth Low Energy, and also send messages in return to a connected device. Simply create a Bluetooth module with a device name of your choice. Received lines are queued and parsed on the main loop, one step later at most. If the main loop is blocked for long and the queue (32 lines) overflows, further lines are dropped and a warning is printed once the main loop continues. Clients uploading many lines at once should therefore pace their writes or wait for a response.

Constructor Description Arguments bluetooth = Bluetooth(device_name) initialize bluetooth with advertised device_name str Properties Description Data type bluetooth.connected Whether a device is currently connected bool bluetooth.last_message_age Time since the last line was received via Bluetooth (ms) int Methods Description Arguments bluetooth.send(data) send data via notification str bluetooth.set_pin(pin) set 6-digit user PIN (000000-999999) int bluetooth.get_pin() print current user PIN or "No user PIN set" bluetooth.reset_pin() remove the user PIN bluetooth.deactivate_pin() Disables PIN enforcement

Lizard will offer a service 23014CCC-4677-4864-B4C1-8F772B373FAC and a characteristic 37107598-7030-46D3-B688-E3664C1712F0 that allows writing Lizard statements like on the command line. On a second characteristic 19f91f52-e3b1-4809-9d71-bc16ecd81069 notifications will be emitted when send(data) is executed.

Access is guarded by a PIN on application level; connections are neither encrypted nor bonded. When a client enables notifications, Lizard sends AUTH_REQUIRED if a PIN is needed and an empty line otherwise. A phone bonded under older firmware gets its subscription restored on connection and can miss this greeting; it can write an empty line instead, which Lizard answers with AUTH_REQUIRED if a PIN is needed. The client then writes AUTH <pin> and receives POST /notification Connected or AUTH_FAIL. Until then, Lizard answers every other line with AUTH_REQUIRED and does not execute it. bluetooth.send(data) does not reach the client before it has entered the PIN either. After three wrong PINs or 30 seconds without a PIN attempt, Lizard closes the connection. The PIN is the user PIN set with bluetooth.set_pin(pin) or, without one, the PIN configured at build time; Lizard prints it on every connection. After bluetooth.deactivate_pin(), every client is accepted without a PIN until the next restart. Note that the PIN is sent unencrypted, so it keeps out accidental connections but not someone listening in.

Unlike core.last_message_age, which any input channel resets, bluetooth.last_message_age only counts lines received via Bluetooth. Together with connected, it lets rules and the host tell a silent or disconnected app apart from a host that keeps talking on UART0. Neither property stops anything by itself; use the wheels' drive_command_timeout for that (see Machine Safety).

docs.title: Serial Bus
docs.text:
The serial bus module lets multiple ESP32s share a UART link with a coordinator that polls peers in turn.

Constructor Description Arguments bus = SerialBus(serial, id) Attach to a serial module with local node id Serial, int Properties Description Data type bus.offset_<id> Estimated clock offset of peer <id> (peer clock minus coordinator clock) in milliseconds, NaN while invalid float bus.offset_<id>_accuracy Error bound of offset_<id> in milliseconds (the true offset lies within offset_<id> ± this value) float bus.telemetry_errors Malformed telemetry frames and layout lines of passed-on or mirrored peers, e.g. with a wrong CRC int bus.telemetry_dropped Telemetry frames of any peer dropped for room in the inbound queue, e.g. while layout lines are awaited int bus.ignored_lines Received lines that are no bus messages and were not printed, e.g. the boot output of a peer int Methods Description Arguments bus.send(receiver, fmt, args...) Send a printf-formatted line to peer receiver (0-254). Specifiers: %d int, %f number (opt. %.Nf), %s string (bool→true/false) int, str, ... bus.make_coordinator(peer_ids...) Set the list of peer IDs, making this node the coordinator ints bus.enable_time_sync() Enable clock offset estimation between coordinator and peers (call on all nodes) bus.pass_telemetry(peer_ids...) Pass the telemetry frames of these peers, or of all peers without IDs, on to the console ints bus.flash_peer(id, boot, enable) Flash peer id through its boot and enable outputs with this node's firmware (see Flashing a Peer) int, 2x Output

The coordinator prints the lines that reach it from its peers, e.g. Ready. and the output of commands sent with bus.send(), with the coordinator's name for the bus and the peer's ID in front, e.g. bus[2]: Ready. for peer 2 of a bus that the coordinator calls bus. So two buses of a node, e.g. plexus and p0, keep their peers apart, also when both have a peer 2.

Polling: The coordinator polls its peers in turn, and a peer answers with the messages it has queued. A poll that its peer does not answer within 250 ms times out with warning: serial bus <name> poll to <id> timed out. The warning comes once until the peer answers again, e.g. after its restart, and then the coordinator prints serial bus <name>: peer <id> answers again after <n> timed out polls.

Other Lines: Lines on the link that are no bus messages are not processed, e.g. the boot output or a panic of a peer, or what a peer prints whose bus has not taken over its console. A coordinator prints those that are readable text, without their Lizard checksum if they have one. With a single peer it prints them as lines of that peer, e.g. bus[2]: Guru Meditation Error: ..., and with several peers, any of which may have sent the line, with only its name for the bus in front, e.g. bus: Guru Meditation Error: .... All others, and all such lines on a peer, are counted in ignored_lines and reported with warning: serial bus <name> ignored <n> lines that are no bus messages, at most once per second. The ROM bootloader and the boot log of a peer always print at 115200 baud, whatever the rate of the link; on a link with another rate they arrive as an unreadable line, so a restart of the peer is followed by one warning about an ignored line.

Time Synchronization: Calling bus.enable_time_sync() on the coordinator and all peers enables passive clock offset estimation on top of the regular poll cycle. The coordinator stamps its local esp_timer clock when it sends a POLL (T1) and when it receives the DONE response (T4), and the peer reports its own receive and send stamps (T2, T3) in the DONE response. Like NTP, the offset is estimated as ((T2 - T1) + (T3 - T4)) / 2, so the peer's processing time between T2 and T3 cancels out, and the remaining unknown transport delay bounds the error of each sample. The coordinator publishes the estimate as the property offset_<id> and its bound as offset_<id>_accuracy. This is intended for timestamping sensor data (e.g. wheel odometry) received from bus peers.

  • Applying it: a peer timestamp t_peer in milliseconds maps to coordinator time as t_peer - offset_<id>; mind the units, since the peer's esp_timer stamps are in microseconds and the properties in milliseconds.
  • Sign: the offset is the peer's clock minus the coordinator's, so it is positive while the peer's esp_timer runs ahead; as both sides count from their own boot, a peer that booted later than the coordinator has a negative offset.
  • Accuracy: each sample's error bound is half the transport time that is not explained by the known airtime of the two frames; samples within 0.5 ms replace the estimate immediately, otherwise the best sample of every 2 s does, so the estimate keeps following crystal drift even on a busy bus. Systematic asymmetries such as RS485 turnaround are not covered by the bound.
  • Validity: the properties are NaN until the first sample arrives and return to NaN whenever the estimate turns invalid, i.e. when the peer's poll times out (e.g. across a peer reboot), or when make_coordinator() or enable_time_sync() is called again, which restarts all estimates. An expander's broadcast carries NaN as the literal nan, so a proxied offset turns NaN as well; the host firmware has to know that literal.
  • Scope: the properties exist only on the coordinator, are created once both make_coordinator() and enable_time_sync() have been called, and stay (as NaN) for IDs dropped from a later list. Referencing them on a peer, before they are created, or for an ID that was never listed is an unknown-property error rather than NaN. Behind an expander, the host learns them with the first broadcast after enable_time_sync(), so a startup script cannot reference them yet. The two properties per peer also count against the coordinator's 1024-byte broadcast line, which overflows at roughly 16 peers; from then on the coordinator reports buffer too small on every step instead of broadcasting any of its properties.
  • Convergence: the first sample after enabling or after a timeout locks the estimate, whatever its bound, within two poll rounds; while polling pauses (e.g. during an OTB update), the estimate freezes and drifts with the crystals until polling resumes.
  • Compatibility: update the coordinator's firmware first, and treat __POLL__<digits> and __DONE__<digits>,<digits>,<digits> payloads as reserved for this protocol. A coordinator sends a sequence number in its POLL only to peers that have answered with a stamped DONE, so peers with older firmware keep working (without an estimate) until they are updated.

Telemetry Frames: A peer that defines telemetry frames with core.telemetry(...) sends them to its own console until a coordinator polls it, and from then on to the coordinator until the peer restarts. A peer whose console is the bus link holds them back until then (see Console as Link). With the first poll the peer sends their layout lines again, this time to the coordinator. While layout lines go to the coordinator, the peer holds back all of its frames. Then it keeps the newest frame of each ID in a slot and sends the slots with the next poll, so a poll delivers the current values and no backlog, and a frame ID arrives at most once per poll of its peer. A frame that is replaced before it was sent does not count in the sequence number, so a gap is still a loss. A peer has eight slots; a frame beyond them is not sent, and the peer warns on its own console and through the coordinator, at most every 10 s. A call that is split into several frames takes one slot per frame; if the slots run out within a call, only its first frames are sent. The frames of a split call arrive as one step only while a poll can carry them within their interval; a peer that sends more than the bus carries delivers steps with some of their frames missing, without a gap in the sequence numbers.

The coordinator checks payloads starting with ~ or __LAYOUT__ and never processes them as Lizard code. bus.pass_telemetry() passes the frames and layout lines of all peers on to the console with the coordinator's name for the bus and the peer's ID in front, here bus[2]:, and bus.pass_telemetry(2) only those of peer 2:

bus = SerialBus(serial, 1)
bus.make_coordinator(2, 3)
bus.pass_telemetry(2)

bus[2]: __LAYOUT__v1 1.0/2 d3 motor.position:f@52
bus[2]: __LAYOUT__v1 1.1/2 d3 motor.enabled:?@76
bus[2]: ~AdMHQOIBALbznT8BIbs=@31

Each call replaces the selection of the previous one; without a call nothing is passed on. Peers send their frames over the bus whether they are passed on or not. The coordinator drops the frames of a peer it neither passes on nor mirrors with a BusTelemetry without checking them. Malformed frames and layout lines of passed-on or mirrored peers, e.g. no valid Base64 or with a wrong CRC, are dropped and counted in telemetry_errors.

  • Recovery: when a frame arrives whose layout the coordinator does not have or that does not match the frame, e.g. because pass_telemetry came after the peer sent its layout lines or the coordinator booted after the peer, it asks the peer for its layout lines with core.telemetry_info(), at most every 2 s. Until the first of them arrives, at most for 2 s, it does not pass the peer's frames on and counts them in telemetry_dropped, since printing the frames queued ahead of the layout lines would keep the inbound queue full and drop those. A BusTelemetry of the peer still gets them. Frames from before the request are passed on anyway, so a reader skips frames whose layout it has not seen yet. When the peer reports Ready., the coordinator forgets its layouts; the peer sends them again with the first poll.
  • Late hosts: core.telemetry_info() on the coordinator also asks every passed-on peer of its make_coordinator list for its layout lines, so a host that connects later gets them too.
  • Queues: a bus keeps the messages of each direction at their length in a queue of 4 KB, and telemetry leaves room for eight of the longest messages free (frames on the coordinator, layout lines on the peer), so commands, their replies and update chunks still get through while frames pile up, e.g. while long prints or the startup block the coordinator. A message takes its length plus 11 to 14 bytes, and a frame is stored without its bus header and checksum, so the room left to telemetry holds 35 frames of 4 floats or 12 frames of 20 floats. Lost telemetry recovers by itself: the next frame replaces a lost one, and missing layout lines are requested again. Frames dropped this way are counted in telemetry_dropped.
  • Bus load: a frame of n floats or ints is a line of about 5.3·n + 25 bytes, on the bus as well as on the coordinator's console. A frame of 20 floats takes 132 bytes, i.e. 2.9 ms at 460800 baud; 100 such frames per second would take almost a third of the bus. The most one poll can carry is all eight slots with the largest frame of 45 floats, about 2.1 KB: 46 ms at 460800 baud, but 180 ms at 115200 baud, close to the coordinator's poll timeout of 250 ms. The room left to telemetry in the coordinator's queue holds six of these frames, so its loop has to take them while they arrive.
  • Console load: the coordinator prints every frame it passes on, and printing blocks its loop until the line is on the wire (see Console load). So every passed-on frame adds its line's time to the coordinator's loop: a frame of 45 floats takes 5.8 ms at 460800 baud, and one of them every 10 ms already needs more than half of the loop. A step handles only the messages that were waiting when it started, so frames that arrive faster than the console prints them slow the loop down instead of stalling it; those that no longer fit into the inbound queue are dropped and counted in telemetry_dropped.
  • Compatibility: update the coordinator's firmware first, since an older coordinator tries to run the peer's frames and layout lines as Lizard code. Payloads starting with ~ or __LAYOUT__ are reserved for telemetry.

Bus Backup: When a SerialBus is created, its configuration (pins, baud rate, UART number, node ID) is automatically saved to non-volatile storage. If multiple SerialBus modules exist, only the first one is backed up. On boot, if the startup script does not create a SerialBus but a backup config exists, Lizard removes all existing Serial modules and recreates the SerialBus from the saved config. This keeps the node reachable over the bus even if a broken script is deployed, avoiding the need for physical USB access. A bus on the console is restored the same way and takes over the console again (see Console as Link). To remove the saved configuration, call core.forget_serial_bus().

Console as Link: A node can use its console UART as a bus link, e.g. a port expander that is wired to the core by its console pins:

serial = Serial(3, 1, 115200, 0)
bus = SerialBus(serial, 2)

A serial on UART0 with the console's RX and TX pins (3 and 1 on an ESP32, 44 and 43 on an ESP32-S3) leaves the console alone until a serial bus is created on it. From then on, only the bus reads and writes UART0, at the serial's baud rate, and the node runs no console lines, only commands from the bus. Everything the node prints goes to the node that polls it, which prints it as a line of this peer, e.g. bus[2]: .... That includes replies, warnings and the output of unmuted modules. Lines printed before the first poll wait in the bus queue; when only the room for eight of the longest messages is free, further lines are dropped and a warning with their number follows. The node does not print Ready. on its console; the coordinator prints it with the first answer, e.g. bus[2]: Ready.. Telemetry frames and their layout lines wait for the first poll. While the bus has the console, ESP-IDF log and ROM output is dropped, but a panic still reaches the wire (see Other Lines). Put the two lines at the top of the startup script, so that the output of the lines below reaches the coordinator, including an error that stops the script. What the node prints before the bus takes over the console still goes out on the console itself, e.g. an error in a line above the two. While the bus backup holds a bus on the console pins, i.e. from the boot after the first one with that bus, the console starts at the bus's baud rate instead of its own, so that the coordinator can read these lines and prints them (see Other Lines). If no bus takes the console over during such a boot, the console returns to its own baud rate before it prints Ready.. A startup script that keeps failing is skipped after two failed boots (see Startup Script); the bus backup then takes over the console again, and the lines the node printed before tell the coordinator why. The console stays silent on USB as long as the startup script or the bus backup creates the bus, also after ./espresso.py flash, which keeps both. To get it back, send the node !-, !. and core.forget_serial_bus() over the bus and restart it, or erase its flash with ./espresso.py erase and flash it again; it then runs at its own baud rate again (see core.set_baudrate()).

Flashing a Peer: A coordinator can flash a peer that is wired to it by the bus's RX and TX pins and by two outputs to the peer's GPIO0 and EN, e.g. a port expander:

serial = Serial(26, 27, 460800, 1)
p0 = SerialBus(serial, 1)
p0.make_coordinator(2)
p0_boot = Output(25)
p0_boot.on()
p0_enable = Output(14)
p0_enable.on()

Keep both outputs on while the peer runs, and turn the boot output on first, so that the peer starts its firmware and not its bootloader. With these lines in the coordinator's startup script, p0.flash_peer(2, p0_boot, p0_enable) flashes the peer, sent once, e.g. from the command line; in the startup script it would flash the peer with every boot. A port expander on a Robot Brain does not run while its enable pin is not driven high.

flash_peer copies this node's firmware onto the peer like expander.flash() at 921600 baud, whatever the link's rate, which erases the peer's NVS, i.e. its startup script, its bus backup and a persisted console baud rate. It needs no answer from the peer, so it also flashes a peer without firmware. It does not check the strapping pins; a peer that does not enter its bootloader fails the transfer before anything is erased. The copy boots with its console at 115200 baud; the coordinator writes it the two lines of a bus on its console as its startup script, with the baud rate of the coordinator's serial and the ID id, and restarts it (see Console as Link). The rest of the peer's startup script goes over the bus, e.g. with configure.py --serial-bus 2 --bus-name p0, which replaces the whole script, so keep the two lines at its top. flash_peer blocks the main loop for the whole transfer like expander.flash(). It fails if another module uses the serial, if boot or enable is no output on a pin of this node, or if the copy does not report Ready. within 5 s. It drives the two pins itself while flashing; afterwards they are high and follow their outputs again, and a peer that a failed transfer left in its bootloader is restarted through its enable pin.

Firmware Updates: Peers on the serial bus can be updated remotely via the coordinator. Use the otb_update.py tool to push new firmware to any peer node. See OTB Update for details.

docs.title: Bus Telemetry
docs.text:
On a serial bus coordinator, a BusTelemetry module mirrors values that one peer sends in its telemetry frames, so that rules, core.output and the coordinator's own frames can use them.

Constructor Description Arguments arm = BusTelemetry(bus, peer_id) Mirror values of peer peer_id SerialBus, int

The module has no properties of its own. Each value it mirrors is a property declaration with the name the peer gives the field:

bus = SerialBus(serial, 1)
bus.make_coordinator(2)
arm = BusTelemetry(bus, 2)
bool arm.motor.enabled = false    # property motor.enabled of peer 2
float arm.motor.position = 0.0
bool arm.parked = false           # variable parked of peer 2
when arm.motor.enabled then wheels.locked = true end
core.telemetry(wheels.linear_speed, arm.motor.position, 100)

Peer 2 has to send these values in one of its frames, e.g. with core.telemetry(motor.position, motor.enabled, parked, 100) in its startup. Two identical peers become two modules, e.g. arm1 = BusTelemetry(bus, 2) and arm2 = BusTelemetry(bus, 3).

  • Declarations: only bool, int and float can be declared. Declaring a name again with the same type only sets the value while no frame has delivered one yet. Another type is an error, and so is the same name of the same peer in a second module, e.g. "motor.position" of peer 2 is already declared by arm.
  • Values: a declared property is read-only. It keeps its declared value until a frame delivers one, and its last value when the peer stops sending or restarts. An int arrives as int32, as at every reader of the frame format, so a value beyond that range wraps around.
  • Layouts: mirroring works whether or not the coordinator passes the peer's frames on. A declaration made later, e.g. at the console, asks the peer for its layout lines again, so the value follows shortly after; the other mirrored values keep following meanwhile. When the peer gives a frame ID to other fields, the module drops the old mapping, so a property does not take the value of another field, and the check for missing names runs again.
  • Warnings: a field the peer sends with another type is not mirrored, and the module warns once, e.g. warning: arm: peer 2 sends "motor.position" as a boolean, not a number. When the peer's frames arrive but none carries a declared name within 5 s, the module warns once, e.g. warning: arm: no frame of peer 2 carries "parked". Both warnings come once per run of the peer, i.e. again after its Ready.. When no frame of the peer arrives within 5 s of a declaration or of the peer's Ready., e.g. because its startup sends none, the peer ID is wrong or the peer is not polled, the module warns once, e.g. warning: arm: no frame of peer 2 within 5 s. A peer whose layout lines have another version than this node reads is not mirrored; the bus warns once per run of the peer, e.g. warning: serial bus bus does not read layout version 2 of peer 2, only version 1, and the module does not report its names as missing.
  • Cost: each mirrored value takes about 100 bytes of heap on the coordinator. Rules over many mirrored values are expensive on their own, so a peer should compute a predicate like parked itself and the coordinator mirror one bool.

docs.title: Input
docs.text:
The input module is associated with a digital input pin that is be connected to a pushbutton, sensor or other input signal.

Constructor Description Arguments input = Input(pin) pin is the corresponding GPIO number int Properties Description Data type input.level Current signal level (0 or 1) int input.change Level change since last cycle (-1..1) int input.inverted Inverts the active property if true bool input.active Current active state of the input bool

Usually, an input is considered active if and only if its level is high. If the inverted property is set to true, the input is considered active if and only if its level is low.

Methods Description input.get() Output the current level input.pullup() Add an internal pull-up resistor input.pulldown() Add an internal pull-down resistor input.pulloff() Remove internal pull resistor

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
The output module is associated with a digital output pin that is connected to an LED, actuator or other output signal.

Constructor Description Arguments output = Output(pin) pin is the corresponding GPIO number int Properties Description Data type output.level Current signal level (0 or 1) int output.change Level change since last cycle (-1..1) int output.enabled Whether the output is enabled bool output.inverted Whether the output is inverted bool output.active Whether the output is active bool

Usually, an output is considered active if and only if its level is high. If the inverted property is set to true, the output is considered active if and only if its level is low.

Methods Description Arguments output.on() Set the output pin high output.off() Set the output pin low output.level(value) Set the output level to the given value bool output.pulse(interval[, duty_cycle]) Switch output on and off floats output.enable() Enable the output output.disable() Disable the output output.activate() Activate the output output.deactivate() Deactivate the output

The pulse() method allows pulsing an output with a given interval in seconds and an optional duty cycle between 0 and 1 (0.5 by default). Note that the pulsing frequency is limited by the main loop to around 20 Hz.

When the output is disabled, it will deactivate and ignore on/off or level commands.

docs.title: PWM Output
docs.text:
The PWM output module is associated with a digital output pin that is connected to an LED, actuator or other output signal.

Constructor Description Arguments pwm = PwmOutput(pin[, lt[, lc]]) pin is the corresponding GPIO number 1–3x int

The constructor arguments lt (LEDC timer) and lc (LEDC channel) are optional and default to 0. When using multiple PWM outputs, set different channel IDs to avoid conflicts. Channels sharing a timer also share its frequency: a new output adopts the timer's frequency, and setting frequency on one output changes it for all of them. Use different timers to run outputs at independent frequencies. The lowest reachable frequency is about 4 Hz on the ESP32 and about 70 Hz on the ESP32-S3; lower values are rejected with an error. On the ESP32-S3 all timers share one clock source, so the 70 Hz are only reachable while no other timer is in use, also none of a StepperMotor. With a second timer running, all frequencies must fit the same source, in practice all above about 306 Hz or all on one timer; a value that needs another source is rejected with an error.

Properties Description Data type pwm.duty Duty cycle (0..256, default: 128) int pwm.frequency Frequency (Hz, 1..312500, default: 1000) int pwm.enabled Whether the output is enabled bool

A PWM period is divided into 256 steps, and duty sets for how many of them the pin stays high. That makes 257 settings, one more than an 8 bit value holds:

duty Output 0 always low 128 high for half of the period 255 high for 255 of 256 steps, not fully on 256 always high Methods Description Arguments pwm.on() Turn on the PWM signal pwm.off() Turn off the PWM signal pwm.enable() Enable the PWM output pwm.disable() Disable the PWM output

When the output is disabled, it will turn off the PWM signal and ignore on/off commands.

docs.title: MCP23017 Port Expander
docs.text:
The MCP23017 allows controlling up to 16 general purpose input or output pins via I2C.

Constructor Description Arguments mcp = Mcp23017([port[, sda[, scl[, address[, clk_speed]]]]]) See below ints

The constructor expects up to five arguments:

  • port: 0 or 1, since the ESP32 has two I2C ports (default: 0)
  • sda: SDA pin (default: 21)
  • scl: SCL pin (default: 22)
  • address: client address of the MCP (0x20..0x28, default: 0x20)
  • clk_speed: I2C clock speed (default: 100000)
Properties Description Data type mcp.levels Levels of all 16 pins int mcp.inputs Input mode of all 16 pins int mcp.pullups Pull-up resistors for all 16 pins int

The properties levels, inputs and pullups contain binary information for all 16 pins in form of a 16 bit unsigned integer.

Methods Description Arguments mcp.levels(value) Set levels of all 16 pins int mcp.inputs(value) Set input mode of all 16 pins int mcp.pullups(value) Set pull-up resistors for all 16 pins int

The methods levels(), inputs() and pullups() expect a 16 bit unsigned integer value containing binary information for all 16 pins.

Use inputs() to configure input and output pins, e.g. inputs(0xffff) all inputs or inputs(0x0000) all outputs. While levels() will only affect output pins, pullups() will only affect the levels of input pins.

Using an MCP23017 port expander module you can not only access individual pins. You can also instantiate the following modules passing the mcp instance as the first argument:

  • Input: input = Input(mcp, pin)
  • Output: output = Output(mcp, pin)
  • Linear motor: motor = LinearMotor(mcp, move_in, move_out, end_in, end_out)

The pins pin, move_in, move_out, end_in and end_out are numbers from 0 to 15 referring to A0...A7 and B0...B7 on the MCP23017.

docs.title: IMU
docs.text:
The IMU module provides access to a Bosch BNO055 9-axis absolute orientation sensor. Currently, only reading the accelerometer is implemented.

Constructor Description Arguments imu = Imu([port[, sda[, scl[, address[, clk_speed]]]]]) See below ints

The constructor expects up to five arguments:

  • port: 0 or 1, since the ESP32 has two I2C ports (default: 0)
  • sda: SDA pin (default: 21)
  • scl: SCL pin (default: 22)
  • address: client address of the MCP (0x28 or 0x29, default: 0x28)
  • clk_speed: I2C clock speed (default: 100000)
Properties Description Data type imu.cal_sys calibration: system (0 to 3) int imu.cal_gyr calibration: gyroscope (0 to 3) int imu.cal_acc calibration: accelerometer (0 to 3) int imu.cal_mag calibration: magnetometer (0 to 3) int imu.acc_x acceleration incl. gravity: x direction (m/s^2) float imu.acc_y acceleration incl. gravity: y direction (m/s^2) float imu.acc_z acceleration incl. gravity: z direction (m/s^2) float imu.mag_x magnetic field strength: x direction (µT) float imu.mag_y magnetic field strength: y direction (µT) float imu.mag_z magnetic field strength: z direction (µT) float imu.gyr_x gyroscope: x direction (degrees/s) float imu.gyr_y gyroscope: y direction (degrees/s) float imu.gyr_z gyroscope: z direction (degrees/s) float imu.yaw orientation: Euler angle yaw (degrees) float imu.roll orientation: Euler angle roll (degrees) float imu.pitch orientation: Euler angle pitch (degrees) float imu.quat_w orientation: quaternion component w float imu.quat_x orientation: quaternion component x float imu.quat_y orientation: quaternion component y float imu.quat_z orientation: quaternion component z float imu.lin_x acceleration excl. gravity: x direction (m/s^2) float imu.lin_y acceleration excl. gravity: y direction (m/s^2) float imu.lin_z acceleration excl. gravity: z direction (m/s^2) float imu.grav_x gravity: x direction (m/s^2) float imu.grav_y gravity: y direction (m/s^2) float imu.grav_z gravity: z direction (m/s^2) float imu.temp temperature (degrees Celsius) int imu.data_select data selection int

The data_select property can be used to select which data is read from the IMU. The default value is 0xffff, which means all data is read. The following bits are available:

  • 0x0001: calibration status
  • 0x0002: accelerometer data
  • 0x0004: magnetometer data
  • 0x0008: gyroscope data
  • 0x0010: Euler angles
  • 0x0020: quaternion
  • 0x0040: linear acceleration
  • 0x0080: gravity
  • 0x0100: temperature

The IMU is read in a background task, so the properties hold the newest completed sample. While reading fails, an error is printed at most once per second and the properties keep their last values. A message is printed when reading works again.

Methods Description Arguments imu.set_mode(mode) Set operation mode of the IMU str

The mode parameter can be one of the following:

Mode Accel Mag Gyro Relative Orientation Absolute Orientation configmode - - - - - acconly X - - - - magonly - X - - - gyroonly - - X - - accmag X X - - - accgyro X - X - - maggyro - X X - - amg X X X - - imu X - X X - compass X X - - X m4g X X X - ndof_fmc_off X X X - X ndof X X X - X

In non-fusion modes (acconly, magonly, gyroonly, accmag, accgyro, maggyro, amg), the sensor signals (Accel, Mag, Gyro) are uncompensated and fusion data (Relative and Absolute Orientation) is not available.

In fusion modes (imu, compass, m4g, ndof_fmc_off, ndof), the sensor signals (Accel, Mag, Gyro) are compensated and fusion data (Relative and Absolute Orientation) is available.

Note that the individual sensors need to be calibrated before the compensated and fused data is accurate.

docs.title: IMU BNO085
docs.text:
The IMU BNO085 module provides access to a Bosch BNO085 9-axis absolute orientation sensor over the shared I²C bus. This module uses the same API as the IMU module but offers improved fusion quality and additional reports.

Note: Only one ImuBno085 instance can be active at a time due to hardware abstraction layer constraints.

Constructor Description Arguments imu = ImuBno085([port[, sda[, scl[, int[, rst[, address[, clk]]]]]]]) See below ints

The constructor expects up to seven arguments:

  • port: I²C port number (default: 0)
  • sda: SDA pin (default matches target, e.g. 21 on ESP32)
  • scl: SCL pin (default matches target, e.g. 22 on ESP32)
  • int: Interrupt pin (default: 26 on ESP32, none on ESP32-S3)
  • rst: Reset pin (default: 32 on ESP32, none on ESP32-S3)
  • address: I²C address (default: 0x4A)
  • clk: I²C clock in Hz (default: 400000)

The properties and methods are similar to the IMU module. The BNO085 offers improved accuracy and better sensor fusion algorithms compared to the BNO055. Unlike the BNO055 module, euler angles (yaw, roll, pitch) are not computed on-device — only quaternion output (quat_w/x/y/z) is provided. Euler conversion should be done upstream. The gyroscope (gyr_x/y/z) is reported in rad/s (the SH2 calibrated gyroscope report), not degrees/s as on the BNO055.

Methods Description Arguments imu.set_mode(mode) Set operation mode of the IMU str

The mode parameter supports the same modes as the IMU module, except ndof_fmc_off (use ndof instead). The configured mode is automatically restored if the BNO085 resets during operation.

Data Select

The data_select property is a bitmask that controls which sensor values are updated each step. It defaults to 0xffff (all enabled). Set individual bits to 0 to skip costly updates you don't need.

Bit Value Data 0 0x0001 Calibration (cal_sys/gyr/acc/mag) 1 0x0002 Accelerometer (acc_x/y/z) 2 0x0004 Magnetometer (mag_x/y/z) 3 0x0008 Gyroscope (gyr_x/y/z) 4 0x0010 Quaternion (quat_w/x/y/z) 5 0x0020 Linear acceleration (lin_x/y/z) 6 0x0040 Gravity (grav_x/y/z) 7 0x0080 Temperature (temp)

Differences to BNO055

The calibration properties (cal_sys, cal_gyr, cal_acc, cal_mag) use the same 0–3 range as the BNO055, but the meaning differs:

Value BNO055 BNO085 0 Not calibrated Unreliable 1 Partially calibrated Low accuracy 2 Mostly calibrated Medium accuracy 3 Fully calibrated High accuracy (fully calibrated)

On the BNO055, cal_sys, cal_gyr, cal_acc, and cal_mag are read together in a single calibration register. On the BNO085, each calibration value is derived from the accuracy status of its corresponding sensor report (e.g. cal_acc is updated when an accelerometer event arrives, cal_sys when a rotation vector event arrives). This means calibration values only update while the corresponding sensor report is enabled via set_mode.

docs.title: CAN interface
docs.text:
The CAN module allows communicating with peripherals on the specified CAN bus.

Constructor Description Arguments can = Can(rx, tx, baud) RX/TX pins and baud rate int, int, int Methods Description Arguments can.send(node_id, d0, d1, d2, d3, d4, d5, d6, d7) Send a frame with 8 data bytes 9x int can.output_extended(mask, code) Print matching 29-bit frames 2x int can.get_status() Print the driver status can.start() Start the driver can.stop() Stop the driver can.reset() Reset the driver

IDs above 0x7FF are sent as extended (29-bit) frames, IDs above 0x1FFFFFFF are rejected. An extended frame with an ID up to 0x7FF cannot be sent; send puts such an ID into a standard frame. Received extended frames never reach other modules, which subscribe to 11-bit IDs only. output_extended(mask, code) prints every extended frame with (id & mask) == code in the same format as the module's output; it can be called several times to add more filters, and code must not have bits outside mask. can.mute() also removes all output_extended filters; unmute() does not bring them back. Extended frames are always printed with an 8-digit hex ID, also after unmute(), so can 00000123,… is an extended and can 123,… a standard frame.

The method get_status() prints the following information:

  • state ("STOPPED", "RUNNING", "BUS_OFF" or "RECOVERING"),
  • msgs_to_tx,
  • msgs_to_rx,
  • tx_error_counter,
  • rx_error_counter,
  • tx_failed_count,
  • rx_missed_count,
  • rx_overrun_count,
  • arb_lost_count and
  • bus_error_count.

After creating a CAN module, the driver is started automatically. The start() and stop() methods are primarily for debugging purposes.

The reset() method will stop the driver, try to recover it and then start it again. It can be used to recover the driver from a "BUS_OFF" state. The module does the same by itself while the bus is "BUS_OFF", at most once per second. It prints "CAN bus running again" once the bus has stayed out of "BUS_OFF" for a second. Each reset sets the counters of get_status() back to zero.

docs.title: Serial interface
docs.text:
The serial module allows communicating with peripherals via the specified connection.

Constructor Description Arguments serial = Serial(rx, tx, baud, num) RX/TX pins, baud rate, UART number 4x int Methods Description Arguments serial.send(b0, b1, b2, ...) Send a number of bytes ints serial.read() Read and output current buffer

This module might be used by other modules that communicate with peripherals via serial. You can, however, unmute the serial module to have incoming messages printed to the command line instead of keeping them buffered for other modules. An unmuted module prints one line per batch of bytes the hardware hands over, so a sender that pauses between its messages gets one line per message. A line carries at most 85 bytes; the rest of a longer batch follows on the next line.

The UART number and its pins stay reserved for the serial module until the core restarts, also after Expander.disconnect().

A serial on UART0 with the console's pins can only carry a serial bus, which takes over the console (see Console as Link); its own methods fail.

docs.title: JBD BMS
docs.text:
The JBD BMS module reads a battery management system with the JBD protocol (frames from 0xDD to 0x77) over a serial, usually at 9600 baud.

Constructor Description Arguments bms = JbdBms(serial) Serial module wired to the BMS Serial Properties Description Data type bms.voltage Total voltage (V) float bms.current Current (A), positive while charging float bms.residual_capacity Remaining capacity (Ah) float bms.nominal_capacity Nominal capacity (Ah) float bms.percentage State of charge (%) int bms.cycles Charge cycles int bms.temperature Mean of the temperature sensors (°C) float bms.protections Protection flags (see below) int bms.fets MOSFETs that are on: charging (bit 0), discharging (bit 1) int bms.cells Number of cells int bms.interval Time between requests (s), 0 to stop them float bms.last_message_age Time since the values were last updated (ms) int bms.errors Answers that were missing or invalid int Methods Description Arguments bms.cell_voltages() Ask for the cell voltages and print them (V) bms.hardware_version() Ask for the hardware version and print it

The module asks for the basic information every interval seconds, 1 s by default, and updates the properties with each valid answer. Until the first valid answer with the basic information, the values of the BMS are 0 and last_message_age counts from the boot, like core.last_message_age. An answer that is missing after 500 ms or invalid, e.g. with a wrong checksum or an error status, counts in errors, and the properties keep their last values. If the answer to a method is missing or invalid, the module also prints a warning, e.g. warning: bms got no cell voltages. Keep the serial muted, since the module reads its bytes.

The bits of protections are:

  • bit 0: cell over-voltage,
  • bit 1: cell under-voltage,
  • bit 2: battery over-voltage,
  • bit 3: battery under-voltage,
  • bit 4: charging over-temperature,
  • bit 5: charging under-temperature,
  • bit 6: discharging over-temperature,
  • bit 7: discharging under-temperature,
  • bit 8: charging over-current,
  • bit 9: discharging over-current,
  • bit 10: short circuit,
  • bit 11: front-end IC error and
  • bit 12: MOSFET software lock.

On a serial bus peer, the values can travel to the coordinator in telemetry frames:

bms_serial = Serial(26, 27, 9600, 2)
bms = JbdBms(bms_serial)
core.telemetry(bms.voltage, bms.current, bms.percentage, bms.temperature, bms.protections, 1000)

docs.title: ODrive Wheels
docs.text:
The ODrive wheels module combines two ODrive motors and provides odometry and steering for differential wheeled robots.

Constructor Description Arguments wheels = ODriveWheels(left_motor, left_motor) Two ODrive motor modules two ODrive motor modules Properties Description Data type wheels.width Wheel distance (m) float wheels.max_wheel_speed Speed limit of the faster wheel in speed() (m/s, 0 = off) float wheels.linear_speed Forward speed (m/s) float wheels.angular_speed Turning speed (rad/s) float wheels.enabled Whether the wheels are enabled bool wheels.locked Whether driving is blocked (safety interlock, see below) bool wheels.drive_command_age Time since the last drive command (ms, see below) int wheels.drive_command_timeout Stop when no drive command arrives for this long (s, 0 = off) float Methods Description Arguments wheels.power(left, right) Move with torque per wheel float, float wheels.speed(linear, angular) Move with linear/angular speed (m/s, rad/s) float, float wheels.off() Turn both motors off (idle state) wheels.enable() Enable both motors wheels.disable() Disable both motors

When the wheels are disabled, they will stop and ignore movement commands. This allows disabling the wheels permanently by setting enabled = false in conjunction with calling the off() method. Now the vehicle can be pushed manually with motors turned off, without taking care of every line of code potentially re-activating the motors.

max_wheel_speed caps speed() at what the drivetrain can do. Driving and turning at once asks the outer wheel for more than either alone; if the drive cut off only that wheel, the robot would veer instead of following the requested curve. So when the faster wheel would exceed max_wheel_speed, both wheels are scaled down together: the robot keeps its direction and curve radius and only gets slower. power() is not limited.

A speed(0, 0) after motion is repeated about every 100 ms for one second, because a single stop can be lost on the bus or refused by a drive, which would leave a wheel creeping at its last setpoint. A further speed(0, 0) restarts the repeat; any other speed(), power() or off() that goes through ends it early, and so do locked, a tripped dead man's switch and disabling the wheels, which hold or stop the wheels on their own. Commands sent to the motors directly are not noticed and get overwritten within that second, so call wheels.off() rather than off() on each motor to idle them right after a stop.

The locked property is a safety interlock for rules running on the microcontroller: while it is true, drive commands are ignored and the wheels are actively held at standstill with a zero-speed setpoint — the motors stay enabled. This lets a rule block driving while some other condition is unmet, for example while a tool is not in its parking position. The hold is sent when locked becomes true and refreshed about once per second, so it re-engages even if a motor controller restarts. locked only blocks commands: disable() still switches the motors off, and a locked but switched-off robot can be pushed by hand. While locked is true, off() does not stick — the hold re-engages within about a second; call disable() to switch the motors off durably. Driving resumes as soon as locked is false again. Writes to locked, enabled, drive_command_timeout and max_wheel_speed are forwarded to shadow modules, so shadowed wheels stop together with their master and keep to the same speed limit.

The drive_command_timeout property is a dead man's switch against lost or silent hosts: after a non-zero speed() or power() command, the wheels stop on their own with a zero-speed setpoint once no further drive command arrived for drive_command_timeout seconds — the motors stay enabled. The stop is always a zero speed, also after power(), so it switches the motors from torque to velocity control. Only speed() and power() count as drive commands; enable(), off() and property writes do not, so they cannot keep a stale motion alive. The stop is logged as a warning and held like locked holds: the zero-speed setpoint is refreshed about once per second, so a stop that did not reach the motors is re-asserted. The next drive command releases the hold and re-arms the switch. The default is 1 s, so a host has to repeat its drive command at least that often to keep driving. Robots driven by a remote control should use a shorter timeout, and 0 disables the switch, e.g. on a test bench. drive_command_age holds the time in milliseconds since the last drive command, whether it was applied or not, for rules that need finer control. See Machine Safety for the background.

Constructor Description Arguments motor = StepperMotor(step, dir[, lt[, lc]]) Step and direction pins 2–4x int

Properties Description Data type motor.position Motor position (steps) int motor.speed Motor speed (steps per second) int motor.idle Motor idle state bool motor.enabled Whether the motor is enabled bool Methods Description Arguments motor.speed(speed[, acceleration]) Move with given speed 2x float motor.position(position, speed[, acceleration]) Move to given position 3x float motor.stop() Stop motor.enable() Enable the motor motor.disable() Disable the motor
